passages.t: A song for the LORD who came in the storm
passages.happening:
“On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang this song” (verse 1). It begins with praise for a people who offered themselves: “When the princes take the lead in Israel, when the people volunteer, bless the LORD” (verse 2).

Then it pictures the LORD coming to fight for his people. “O LORD, when You went out from Seir, when You marched from the land of Edom, the earth trembled, the heavens poured out rain, and the clouds poured down water” (verse 4). The mountains shake before ‘the One of Sinai’ (verse 5).

The song remembers how bad things had been. In the days of Shamgar and of Jael, the roads were empty and travelers kept to back paths. “Life in the villages ceased; it ended in Israel, until I, Deborah, arose, a mother in Israel” (verse 7). When Israel chose new gods, war came to its gates, and there was hardly a shield or a spear among forty thousand (verse 8).

So the song calls everyone, the rich who ride white donkeys and the poor who walk the road, to listen to the singers at the wells, who ‘shall recount the righteous acts of the LORD’ (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 4 told the victory as a story. Chapter 5 sings it. Many scholars think this song is one of the oldest pieces of Hebrew writing, composed perhaps not long after the battle, around the twelfth century BC on the usual dating. Its Hebrew is old and difficult in places, with rare words and old forms, which is why translations differ so much in verses 10 to 15. Others argue that an old style can be imitated and prefer a later date. Most hold that the song is early.

Victory songs sung by women were part of Israel's life. Miriam led the women with tambourines after the Red Sea, and later the women sang when David came home from battle.

Hebrew poetry works by pairs of lines. The second line repeats, extends or sharpens the first. Listen for it: ‘the earth trembled’, then ‘the heavens poured out rain’, then ‘the clouds poured down water’.

The picture of the LORD marching from Seir and Edom, in the south, draws on an old memory that God came from the region of Sinai to help his people. It also sets the LORD against Baal, the storm god of Canaan. In this song it is Israel's God who sends the rain and the flood.

‘A mother in Israel’ is a title of honor and care. It speaks of Deborah's care for a whole people in danger.

Verse 8 gives the cause of the trouble in a few words: ‘When they chose new gods, then war came to their gates.’

The singers at the watering places are a picture of how stories were kept in a world where few could read. People gathered at the wells to draw water, and there the saving deeds of God were told again and again. ‘Righteous acts’ means the deeds by which God put things right for people who were being wronged.
passages.later:
Other songs and prayers remember God coming from the south in storm and earthquake: “The LORD came from Sinai and dawned upon us from Seir” (Deuteronomy 33:2); “the earth shook and the heavens poured down rain before God, the One on Sinai” (Psalm 68:8); “God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran” (Habakkuk 3:3).

Deborah's song stands beside the song at the sea, where Miriam sang, “Sing to the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and rider He has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:21).
passages.asks: The song begins by honoring the people who offered themselves. Ask where God is asking you to volunteer rather than wait to be pressed. And think of the singers at the wells. Ask where in your ordinary week you tell what God has done, so that the people around you hear it.

passages.t: The roll call of the tribes
passages.happening:
The song calls on Deborah to wake and sing, and on Barak to take his captives (verse 12). Then it names who came to the battle and who did not.

Ephraim came, and Benjamin. Commanders came down from Machir, a clan of Manasseh. Zebulun came, and the princes of Issachar were with Deborah (verses 13-15).

Others held back. ‘In the clans of Reuben there was great indecision’ (verse 15). “Why did you sit among the sheepfolds to hear the whistling for the flocks?” (verse 16). “Gilead remained beyond the Jordan. Dan, why did you linger by the ships? Asher stayed at the coast and remained in his harbors” (verse 17).

“Zebulun was a people who risked their lives; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the battlefield” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
This roll call gives a rare picture of Israel before it had a king. The tribes were a loose alliance, and going to war was voluntary. No king could order them out. Each tribe chose whether to come.

Ten tribes or clans are named. Six came: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali. Four did not: Reuben; Gilead, meaning the tribes east of the Jordan; Dan; and Asher. Judah and Simeon are not mentioned at all, perhaps because they were too far south, or not yet closely bound to the northern tribes.

The song does not curse the tribes that stayed home. It asks them questions, sharp ones. Reuben sat listening to the shepherds' pipes. Dan lingered by the ships. Asher stayed in its harbors. They had their reasons, and their reasons were their own comfort and safety.

Against them stand Zebulun and Naphtali, who ‘risked their lives’. The word for those who volunteered, at the start of the song, is the same word used for a freewill offering. The victory depended on people who gave themselves.
passages.later:
Jacob's last words over his sons had said that Reuben would not excel, and the notes on Genesis 49 read this verse as part of that story: “Why did you sit among the sheepfolds to hear the whistling for the flocks?” (Judges 5:16). Moses' words over the tribes ask only, “Let Reuben live and not die” (Deuteronomy 33:6).

The New Testament pictures God's people as a body whose members belong to one another: “If one part suffers, every part suffers with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26).
passages.asks: Some tribes risked their lives, and some stayed with their sheep and their ships. Ask where others in God's family are in a fight that you could join, and what keeps you by your own sheepfolds. And ask whether your reasons for staying home would sound as good if they were sung back to you.

passages.happening:
“Kings came and fought; then the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo, but they took no plunder of silver” (verse 19).

“From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera. The River Kishon swept them away, the ancient river, the River Kishon” (verses 20-21). The hooves of the horses thunder as they gallop (verse 22).

The angel of the LORD curses the town of Meroz, ‘for they did not come to help the LORD’ (verse 23).

Then the song turns to Jael. “Most blessed among women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, most blessed of tent-dwelling women” (verse 24). “He asked for water, and she gave him milk. In a magnificent bowl she brought him curds” (verse 25). The song tells his death in short, repeated lines: ‘At her feet he collapsed, he fell, there he lay still’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The battle was fought in the Jezreel Valley, near Taanach and Megiddo. The kings came for plunder and took none.

The song adds what the prose account of chapter 4 did not say. The stars fought, and the River Kishon swept the enemy away. Read as poetry, it means that heaven itself fought for Israel. Many readers take it to mean that a sudden storm flooded the river and turned the plain to mud, so that the chariots were useless.

Meroz is otherwise unknown. Its sin was to stay away. The curse is spoken against a town of Israel that would not come to help, and it is spoken by the angel of the LORD. Standing apart from God's people in their need was treated as a serious wrong.

The verses about Jael are built in a way typical of very old Hebrew poetry, a staircase: a phrase is said, then repeated and built on. ‘He collapsed, he fell’ comes again and again, so that the fall of the great commander is told slowly, line by line.

The song gives Jael its highest praise. It is a song of an oppressed people who had been rescued, and it praises the woman through whom the rescue came. Chapter 4's note sets out how readers have weighed her act: as a choice for God's people in war against a brutal enemy, as a deed the song celebrates for the rescue it brought without passing full judgment on its means, or as a breach of the trust owed to a guest by a man who had himself broken custom. These notes do not choose among them.
passages.later:
Joshua's long day is remembered in language like this, of heaven joining the battle (Joshua 10:12-14), and a later psalm asks God to act again ‘as to Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon’ (Psalm 83:9).

Luke's Gospel echoes the praise of Jael when Elizabeth greets Mary: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1:42). Jael was a woman through whom God rescued his people. Mary is too, but by giving birth and not by a sword.
passages.asks: Meroz is remembered only for staying away. Ask whether there is a need among God's people that you have quietly avoided, and what it would cost you to come. And notice how the song tells the fall of a strong man slowly, line by line. Ask what strength you lean on that could fail as suddenly as Sisera's.

passages.happening:
The song ends in an unexpected place, the house of the enemy. “Sisera’s mother looked through the window; she peered through the lattice and lamented: ‘Why is his chariot so long in coming? What has delayed the clatter of his chariots?’” (verse 28).

Her wisest ladies answer, and she keeps telling herself the same thing (verse 29). Surely the men are dividing the spoil: a girl or two for each soldier, and fine dyed and embroidered cloth for Sisera (verse 30).

Then the song closes with a prayer. “So may all Your enemies perish, O LORD! But may those who love You shine like the sun at its brightest.” And the land had rest for forty years (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The reader knows what Sisera's mother does not. Her son is dead in a tent. She and her ladies imagine him dividing the plunder.

The plunder they imagine is the same thing Israel had suffered under him for twenty years: women taken as captives and goods carried off. The Hebrew words translated ‘a girl or two’ are a crude soldier's expression for captive women. The ugly phrase shows what Sisera's victories had meant for Israel's daughters, and why his defeat was a rescue.

The song began with one mother, Deborah, a mother in Israel. It ends with another mother, waiting at a window for a son who will not come home. The two mothers stand on opposite sides of the same day.

The closing prayer asks that God's enemies perish and that those who love him shine like the sun. The land then has rest for forty years.
passages.later: Jesus gave a further command for the way his followers are to regard their enemies: “But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). And God's own word on the death even of the wicked is this: “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD. Wouldn’t I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23).
passages.hard:
How can a song in Scripture seem to gloat over a man's death and mock his grieving mother?

The ending is unsettling, and some readers hear cruelty in it.

Others hear something more complex. The scene exposes what lay behind Sisera's glory. His mother imagines captured Israelite women and plunder, the very things Israel had suffered under him. The irony turns the oppressor's own violence back on him. Some interpreters also hear a note of pity in the picture of a mother waiting at a window.

The song was written from the side of an oppressed people rejoicing that they had been freed, and Scripture keeps such songs honestly. Later Scripture, and above all Jesus' command to love enemies, sets a further light on how God's people are to regard even those who have harmed them. The song is part of the Bible's story. It is not the Bible's last word on enemies.
passages.asks: The song asks the reader to look through a window into the enemy's house. Ask whether you have ever let yourself see the people on the other side of a conflict as people, with mothers who wait for them. And ask how the prayer ‘may those who love You shine like the sun’ might be answered in you, toward people you would rather see fall.
